Topic: KV cache fragmentation and eviction thrashing in paged attention systems under bursty multi-tenant request concurrency

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-3764)
response:
The central question is: when multiple tenants simultaneously submit requests with heterogeneous context lengths and arrival patterns, how does a paged attention system allocate, share, and reclaim KV cache blocks without inducing eviction cascades that serialize what should be parallel execution? Paged attention divides the KV cache into fixed-size blocks (typically 16–32 tokens) allocated on demand, enabling non-contiguous storage and prefix sharing across requests — but the block granularity creates internal fragmentation (a request consuming 17 tokens still holds a full 32-token block) and the eviction policy must decide, under pressure, which partially-filled or mid-sequence blocks to reclaim without stalling the requests that own them. The expert worry that beginners entirely miss is eviction thrashing: under bursty concurrency, a naive LRU policy evicts blocks from requests that are merely waiting for the next decode step, only to have those same requests immediately re-prefill the evicted content when scheduled again — turning a memory pressure problem into a catastrophic compute problem, because re-prefill is O(n²) in sequence length relative to O(n) for a decode step. A second expert concern is prefix sharing invalidation: when a shared prefix block is evicted to satisfy one tenant's allocation, every other tenant whose KV cache was built on that shared prefix suddenly has a broken reference chain, forcing cascading re-prefills across multiple independent requests simultaneously. The interaction between block granularity, eviction timing, and scheduler visibility is what makes this hard — the memory manager and the request scheduler must be jointly aware of which requests are decode-phase vs. prefill-phase, how much each block is shared, and what the re-prefill cost of eviction actually is, yet most systems treat these as separate subsystems with no shared cost model.

NEXT: Given that re-prefill cost is O(n²) in sequence length, what specific information would an optimal eviction policy need to expose to the scheduler to avoid evicting blocks whose re-prefill cost exceeds the marginal throughput gain from freeing them?

An optimal eviction policy needs to expose at minimum four quantities per block: (1) re-prefill cost — the sequence length of the owning request squared, scaled by the model's prefill throughput (e.g., on an A100 with a 70B model, re-prefilling 2K tokens costs ~200ms vs. ~2ms for a single decode step, a 100× penalty); (2) block reuse probability — for shared prefix blocks, the number of active requests referencing that block and the historical hit rate for that prefix hash, which vLLM tracks via its radix-tree prefix cache but does not feed back into eviction cost estimates; (3) time-to-next-schedule — how far in the future the owning request is expected to be scheduled again, because evicting a block from a request that will be scheduled in the next 5ms is almost always a net loss; and (4) marginal memory yield — how many contiguous free blocks the eviction actually produces, since evicting one block from a fragmented allocation often fails to satisfy the incoming request's contiguous-block requirement anyway. The Preble system (2024, OSDI) and the MemServe paper both move toward exposing reuse-aware cost signals, but neither constructs a full cost-benefit ratio of the form re-prefill_cost / (blocks_freed × expected_utilization_gain) before committing to eviction. The scheduler also needs to know whether a candidate eviction would break a shared prefix chain — a single eviction that invalidates a 512-token shared prefix referenced by 8 concurrent requests multiplies the re-prefill cost by 8, yet a block-level LRU sees only one block. Without a dependency graph over block sharing relationships plus a live estimate of each request's scheduling urgency, the eviction policy is operating on a strict subset of the information needed to make non-regret decisions.

The copy-offload decision reduces to comparing three latencies: PCIe transfer time for the block, NVMe read latency if a second eviction pushes it further, and re-prefill compute cost — and the crossover is highly sensitive to sharing fanout. A single KV block of 32 tokens in a 70B model (GQA with 8 KV heads, fp16) occupies roughly 32 × 8 × 2 × 128 × 2 bytes ≈ 1MB per layer × 80 layers = ~80MB for the full prefix block stack; copying that over PCIe 4.0 (≈28 GB/s practical) costs ~3ms, while re-prefilling 512 tokens on an A100 costs ~50ms at typical serving throughput — so offload wins at fanout=1 if the block will be reused even once before the copy is evicted from CPU DRAM. The break-even calculation shifts dramatically with sequence length: for a 4K-token shared prefix, re-prefill costs scale to ~800ms (quadratic), making even NVMe offload (latency ~100–200μs for sequential reads at block granularity, but ~500ms for the full 80-layer transfer at NVMe bandwidth of ~6 GB/s) competitive only if the block is reused by 2+ tenants before the next eviction wave. Inferring from the InfiniGen (2024) and CacheGen papers, systems that compress KV cache before offload (CacheGen achieves ~4× compression via quantization to int4 + entropy coding) can shift the PCIe transfer cost down to ~20MB/prefix block, making CPU DRAM offload strictly dominant over re-prefill for any shared prefix longer than ~200 tokens with fanout ≥ 2. The critical non-obvious failure mode is offload queue saturation: under bursty concurrency, dozens of requests simultaneously trigger prefix eviction, and the PCIe bus becomes the bottleneck — DistServe and Mooncake both report that naive async offload degrades to synchronous blocking when the offload queue depth exceeds ~4 concurrent transfers, eliminating the latency benefit entirely. The practical break-even therefore isn't a fixed sequence length but a joint threshold: offload dominates when fanout × re-prefill_cost > transfer_cost + queue_wait_time, and any production system needs to estimate queue wait time dynamically rather than treating PCIe bandwidth as always available.

The core primitive needed is a backpressure signal that propagates offload queue depth upstream into the admission controller before the queue saturates — concretely, the scheduler should treat the offload queue as a first-class resource with a capacity budget, rejecting or delaying new prefill scheduling when queue occupancy exceeds a threshold (Mooncake's disaggregated architecture exposes exactly this kind of transfer-layer backpressure, though it targets prefill-decode disaggregation rather than eviction offload specifically). A second primitive is priority-tiered offload: not all blocks are equally urgent to copy, so the system should maintain a scored offload queue ordered by fanout × expected_reuse_probability × sequence_length, draining highest-value blocks first and simply evicting (accepting re-prefill) for low-fanout short blocks when the queue is under pressure — this converts the binary copy-or-evict decision into a continuous priority problem that gracefully degrades. Prefill pacing is the third primitive: instead of admitting all queued prefill requests simultaneously during a burst, the scheduler releases them in rate-limited waves sized to keep new KV block allocation below the rate at which the offload pipeline can drain existing eviction candidates, a technique analogous to TCP congestion control's slow-start but applied to memory pressure rather than network bandwidth. The Sarathi-Serve chunked-prefill approach (2024) provides a natural hook here — by splitting prefill into fixed-size chunks (e.g., 512 tokens per scheduling step), it gives the system discrete opportunities between chunks to check offload queue depth and throttle further prefill admission without fully stalling the request. What remains largely unsolved is proactive eviction: rather than waiting for allocation pressure to trigger eviction, the system could speculatively offload blocks from requests predicted to be idle (e.g., requests awaiting tool-call returns or user think-time) before pressure materializes, using request-state signals the application layer knows but the KV cache manager typically cannot see. Systems like Preble gesture toward cross-request state visibility, but closing the loop between application-layer request lifecycle signals and the memory manager's proactive offload decisions remains an open engineering gap in production LLM serving stacks.

When backpressure forces a chunk stall mid-prefill, the latency distribution develops a bimodal shape: requests that complete prefill before the stall land near the baseline TTFT, while requests caught mid-prefill accumulate stall time proportional to how many chunks remain, producing a heavy right tail — in Sarathi-Serve's own evaluation, chunked prefill already introduces inter-chunk scheduling jitter of 10–30ms per chunk on A100s under mixed workloads, and a backpressure-induced stall multiplies this by however many scheduling rounds the system needs to drain the offload queue. The stall-versus-preempt decision should hinge on three factors: (1) sunk prefill cost — a request that is 80% through a 4K-token prefill has already paid ~640ms of compute (at typical A100 throughput); preempting it discards that work and re-prefill cost is now only 20% avoided, making stall almost always preferable beyond a completion threshold of ~60–70%; (2) block pool criticality — if the system is within one or two blocks of total exhaustion, the marginal value of recovering even partially-used blocks outweighs the sunk cost argument, because a fully stalled system produces zero throughput for all requests; (3) estimated remaining prefill time versus estimated queue drain time — if the offload queue will clear in 50ms but the remaining prefill takes 200ms, stalling is strictly dominated by preemption-with-offload of the partial KV state. The partial-state offload case is particularly under-explored: vLLM's preemption today discards mid-prefill KV state entirely (re-prefill from token 0), but a system that could checkpoint partial prefill state to CPU DRAM would convert preemption from a full re-prefill penalty into a partial one, recovering only the evicted blocks' worth of compute — though this requires the attention kernel to support non-zero KV state initialization, which neither FlashAttention-2 nor FlashAttention-3 exposes as a first-class operation. A practical scheduler heuristic used in some production systems (reported anecdotally from Meta's and Databricks' serving teams) is a completion ratio threshold of ~0.75: requests past 75% of their estimated prefill length are always stalled rather than preempted, while requests below 25% are preemption candidates if block pressure is severe, with the middle band resolved by a cost-benefit ratio computed per scheduling tick. The deeper problem is that the scheduler needs an accurate prefill length estimate to apply any of these thresholds — for requests where the full prompt length is known upfront (batch inference), this is trivial, but for interactive multi-turn sessions where the user's next message length is unknown, the system must either over-provision blocks speculatively or accept that preemption decisions are made under uncertainty about sunk cost.

Beyond prompt length, the richest signal is request metadata the application layer already possesses but rarely forwards: whether the system prompt contains tool definitions (a strong predictor of imminent tool-call interruption), the turn index in a multi-turn session (early turns in agentic workflows have empirically higher tool-call rates than late turns, where the model is typically synthesizing a final answer), and the presence of structured output constraints (JSON schema forcing, function-call grammars) which correlate with short decode phases followed by immediate re-entry. Token-level early-exit signals offer a second class of predictors: the model's own generation during the first 5–10 decode tokens often reveals whether it is entering a tool-call trajectory (the token sequence {"tool": or <function_call> appearing within the first 3 tokens with >0.95 probability in models fine-tuned for tool use) — a scheduler that speculatively peeks at the first decoded token distribution could classify the request into decode-bound versus tool-interrupt with high confidence before committing to block retention. Session-level historical statistics are a third signal: in production traces from Anthropic and OpenAI-style deployments, individual users exhibit strong bimodal think-time distributions — either responding in under 2 seconds (continuation) or over 30 seconds (distraction/context switch) — meaning a session's prior inter-turn latencies are predictive of whether the current gap will be short or long, exactly the signal needed to decide whether to hold KV blocks in GPU SRAM, offload to CPU DRAM, or evict entirely. The prediction changes the preemption calculus asymmetrically: a request classified as decode-imminent should have its blocks protected even under moderate memory pressure (the cost of eviction is full re-prefill within milliseconds), while a tool-interrupt-likely request should be proactively offloaded to CPU DRAM during the tool execution gap rather than waiting for pressure to force eviction, since the offload can proceed asynchronously while the tool call is in flight — this is the core insight behind RAGCache and the KV cache-aware scheduling in Preble, though neither fully closes the loop with live session-state signals. What remains unaddressed in published systems is cross-layer signal propagation: the application framework (LangChain, LlamaIndex, custom agentic loops) knows the tool call has been dispatched and its expected latency (a web search tool returns in ~500ms, a database query in ~50ms), but this information sits entirely above the serving layer and never reaches the KV cache manager — the API boundary between application and inference engine is the structural reason proactive offload remains reactive in practice, and closing it would require either a richer serving API (exposing hints like expected_idle_ms) or in-process deployment where the application and engine share memory.

The minimal extension is a session hint header — a small, optional metadata envelope attached to each request that carries three fields: session_id (a stable token identifying the conversation, already present in some deployments for routing affinity), expected_idle_ms (an integer estimate of how long before the next request in this session will arrive, provided by the application framework at tool-dispatch time), and kv_retention_tier (an explicit hint: hot, warm, or evictable, mapping to GPU SRAM, CPU DRAM, and free-pool respectively) — none of which require the server to maintain per-session state, since the hints are interpreted statelessly per request and the server remains free to ignore them under pressure. The stateless constraint is preserved because these hints are advisory, not contractual: the serving engine treats expected_idle_ms=500 as a soft signal that adjusts eviction priority scores rather than a hard reservation that must be honored, exactly analogous to HTTP's Cache-Control headers which carry caching intent without obligating any specific cache behavior. The session_id field already exists informally in several production deployments — Anthropic's internal tooling, Azure OpenAI's user field, and vLLM's --enable-prefix-caching all use some form of session affinity for routing — but none of these systems propagate the identifier down into the KV cache eviction layer, stopping instead at the load balancer; the extension here is purely about depth of propagation, not a new concept. A second minimal extension is a stream_hint: tool_call_imminent flag on the response side: when the model's token distribution indicates a tool call is about to be emitted (detectable at the serving layer with negligible overhead by checking the top-1 token against a tool-call token set), the server proactively initiates async offload of the session's KV blocks before the tool call completes, giving a ~500ms head start on the transfer that typically covers the full PCIe copy cost for sessions under 8K tokens. The horizontal scaling concern dissolves if session_id is used only for within-request decisions (eviction priority on the node currently holding the request) rather than for cross-node affinity routing — the latter requires sticky sessions and breaks load balancing, but the former requires no coordination at all, since each node independently interprets the hint against its own local memory pressure without communicating with peers. The outstanding design tension is hint freshness under rerouting: if a request is rerouted to a different node (due to node failure or load rebalancing), the new node has no KV cache for that session and the kv_retention_tier: hot hint is meaningless — which argues for pairing session hints with a lightweight KV cache existence registry (a Redis-style sidecar mapping session IDs to node addresses and tier locations) so the receiving node can pull the offloaded blocks rather than re-prefilling from scratch.

The registry only needs eventual consistency with bounded staleness — not strong consistency — because a stale registry entry produces a cache miss (the node fetches blocks that have already been evicted) rather than a correctness violation; the worst outcome is unnecessary re-prefill, not corrupted model state, which means the system can tolerate registry lag of hundreds of milliseconds without affecting output correctness. The critical guarantee is monotonic eviction propagation: when a node evicts or downgrades a block (GPU→CPU→evicted), that transition must eventually reach the registry before the block's absence causes a fetch attempt to a dead location — a liveness property rather than a safety one — and a tombstone TTL approach (eviction writes a deleted marker with a 2-second TTL rather than immediately removing the entry) handles most races without requiring distributed transactions. The nastiest failure mode is an eviction race under node failure: node A holds a session's KV blocks in CPU DRAM, the registry reflects this, node A crashes, a new request for that session arrives at node B which reads the registry and attempts to pull the blocks from node A's address — the pull times out after ~100ms (typical gRPC deadline), node B falls back to re-prefill, but meanwhile the registry still shows node A as the owner for another 30 seconds (until the heartbeat TTL expires), so every subsequent request for that session pays the 100ms timeout penalty before re-prefilling. A second failure mode is phantom promotion: node A offloads blocks to CPU DRAM and updates the registry to warm, then under continued pressure evicts them entirely but crashes before writing the evicted tombstone — the registry permanently shows warm for a block that no longer exists anywhere, and any node that trusts the registry will attempt a fetch that returns 404, requiring a fallback path that most systems do not implement cleanly. Mooncake's disaggregated architecture partially addresses this by treating the transfer layer as a best-effort service with explicit fallback to re-prefill on any fetch failure, effectively making the registry an optimization hint rather than a source of truth — this is the right abstraction, but it requires every consumer of registry data to implement the fallback path, and production experience (from Alibaba's PAI-Blade and ByteDance's LLM serving teams) shows that fallback paths are systematically undertested and fail in correlated ways during the exact node-failure bursts when they are most needed. The correct engineering response is to treat the registry as a probabilistic cache directory with explicit uncertainty: entries carry a confidence score that decays with time since last heartbeat, and the scheduler uses that score to decide whether to speculatively initiate re-prefill in parallel with a fetch attempt — a hedged request pattern analogous to Jeff Dean's tail-latency hedging, where the re-prefill is cancelled if the fetch succeeds within a deadline but completes otherwise.
